title: Probability up to a point
objectives: Read and use a cumulative distribution function.
Find interval chances, tail chances and the pmf from a CDF.

screens.prose: Toss a fair coin three times, and let $X$ be the number of heads. Its pmf, from the last lesson, is drawn below.

state.caption: The pmf of $X$, the number of heads in three tosses

screens.question: What is the chance of at most one head, $P(X \le 1)$?

widget.label: Chance of at most one head

hints.text: Which values of $X$ are at most 1?
Two bars count: no heads and one head.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the bars for every value up to and including 1.

byKey.one-only: That is $p(1)$ alone. At most one head includes no heads at all.
byKey.zero-only: That is $p(0)$ alone. Exactly one head also counts as at most one.
byKey.at-least: That is the chance of at least one head. At most one means 0 or 1.

explain.text: At most one head means $X = 0$ or $X = 1$. You add those two bars: $\tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Next we keep adding bars as the cut-off moves right.

screens.prose: Now let the cut-off move. For each $x$, the height of the graph is $P(X \le x)$: every bar at or left of $x$, added up. Slide $x$ from left to right.
screens.question: Where does the height jump?

options.text: At 0, 1, 2 and 3: the values $X$ can take

options.why: Between 1 and 2 nothing new can happen, since $X$ is never 1.5. So the height stays flat there.
At 1.5 no new bar is added. The height changes only when $x$ reaches a value $X$ can take.

hints.text: Slide slowly from 1.9 to 2.0. What changes?

feedback.correct: The height jumps only when $x$ reaches a new value of $X$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the caption as $x$ crosses each whole number.

explain.text: The height is flat between whole numbers and jumps at 0, 1, 2 and 3. Each jump adds one bar: $\tfrac{1}{8}$, $\tfrac{3}{8}$, $\tfrac{3}{8}$, $\tfrac{1}{8}$. At $x = 2$ itself the height is already $\tfrac{7}{8}$, because $X \le 2$ includes $X = 2$.

screens.prose: The height you read is the **cumulative distribution function**, or **CDF**, of $X$: $$F(x) = P(X \le x).$$ The closed dots show that at a value, $F$ already includes it.
screens.question: What is $F(2.4)$?

hints.text: Which values of $X$ are at most 2.4?
Read the height of the step above 2.4.
$X \le 2.4$ means $X = 0, 1$ or $2$. Add $\tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{3}{8} + \tfrac{3}{8}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add every bar at or left of 2.4.

byKey.bar: That is $p(2)$, one bar. $F$ adds every bar up to 2.4, so 0 and 1 count too.
byKey.below-two: You stopped before 2. $X = 2$ is at most 2.4, so its bar counts.
byKey.zero: $X$ is never exactly 2.4, but $F$ asks for $X \le 2.4$, which happens often.

explain.text: $X$ cannot be 2.4, but $X \le 2.4$ holds whenever $X$ is 0, 1 or 2. So $F(2.4) = \tfrac{7}{8}$, the same as $F(2)$. Between values, $F$ stays flat.

screens.prose: A CDF answers more than at-most questions. Use two heights from the graph.
screens.question: What is $P(1 < X \le 3)$?

widget.label: Chance X is above 1 and at most 3

hints.text: Which values of $X$ lie above 1 and at most 3?
Read $F(3)$ and $F(1)$ off the graph.
$X \le 3$ always, and $X \le 1$ has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Take one from the other.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the height at 3 and subtract the height at 1.

byKey.incl-one: You included $X = 1$. The interval $1 < X$ starts just above 1.
byKey.upper: That is $F(3)$ alone. Remove the chance that $X$ is 1 or less.
byKey.two-only: That is $p(2)$. $X = 3$ also lies in the range.

explain.text: $X \le 3$ splits into $X \le 1$ and $1 < X \le 3$. So $P(1 < X \le 3) = F(3) - F(1) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Check with the bars: $p(2) + p(3) = \tfrac{3}{8} + \tfrac{1}{8}$.

screens.prose: Now an at-least question. The graph only gives at-most chances, so think about what is left over.
screens.question: What is $P(X > 2)$?

hints.text: $X > 2$ and $X \le 2$ cannot both happen, and one of them must.
Read the height at 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the height at 2 away from 1.

byKey.height: That is $F(2) = P(X \le 2)$, the opposite event. Take it away from 1.
byKey.ge: You used $1 - F(1)$, which is $P(X \ge 2)$. $X > 2$ leaves out $X = 2$.

explain.text: $X > 2$ is the complement of $X \le 2$. So $P(X > 2) = 1 - F(2) = 1 - \tfrac{7}{8} = \tfrac{1}{8}$, which is $p(3)$: three heads.

explain.text: The larger die is at most 4 exactly when both dice are. That is a 4 by 4 square, so $F(4) = \tfrac{16}{36}$. The same argument gives $F(y) = \tfrac{y^2}{36}$ for $y = 1, \dots, 6$.

screens.prose: Here is the CDF of $Y$. Each step is a square of cells over 36: $\tfrac{1}{36}, \tfrac{4}{36}, \tfrac{9}{36}$ and so on, up to 1.
screens.question: Use the jump at 4 to find $P(Y = 4)$.

hints.text: How high is the graph just before 4, and at 4?
Look at the steps either side of 4.
The graph goes from $\tfrac{9}{36}$ to $\tfrac{16}{36}$ at 4. The jump is the difference.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the height just before 4 from the height at 4.

byKey.height: That is $F(4)$, the height. $P(Y = 4)$ is the size of the jump at 4.
byKey.values: You treated the six values of $Y$ as equally likely. Read the jump instead.
byKey.below: That is $F(3)$, the height before the jump. Subtract it from $F(4)$.

explain.text: The graph jumps from $\tfrac{9}{36}$ to $\tfrac{16}{36}$ at 4, a jump of $\tfrac{7}{36}$. That is the L of 7 cells from the first lesson. Every jump of a CDF is a bar of the pmf.

screens.prose: Same CDF of $Y$. This time both ends of the range are included.
screens.question: What is $P(2 \le Y \le 4)$?

options.why: You computed $F(4) - F(2)$. That is $P(2 < Y \le 4)$: it drops $Y = 2$, which has chance $\tfrac{3}{36}$.
That is $F(4) = P(Y \le 4)$. It still includes $Y = 1$.
That is $P(Y = 4)$ alone. $Y = 2$ and $Y = 3$ are in the range too.

hints.text: Which values of $Y$ are in the range?
$Y = 2$ is in the range. Which height still contains it?
Subtract the height just below 2, which is $F(1) = \tfrac{1}{36}$: $\tfrac{16}{36} - \tfrac{1}{36}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep $Y = 2$, 3 and 4, and remove only $Y = 1$.

byKey.minus-a: You computed $F(4) - F(2)$. That drops $Y = 2$, which has chance $\tfrac{3}{36}$. Subtract $F(1)$ instead.

explain.text: $F(4) - F(2)$ removes everything up to and including 2, so $Y = 2$ is lost. To keep it, subtract the height just below 2: $F(4) - F(1) = \tfrac{15}{36}$. Check: $p(2) + p(3) + p(4) = \tfrac{3 + 5 + 7}{36}$.

screens.prose: You have been subtracting heights. Here is why $$P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)$$ holds for any $a < b$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: $\{X \le b\} = \{X \le a\} \cup \{a < X \le b\}$, since $a < b$
No value is both $\le a$ and $> a$, so the two pieces are disjoint
Add chances of disjoint events: $F(b) = F(a) + P(a < X \le b)$

hints.text: Start by cutting the event $X \le b$ at $a$.
Before you add chances, you need the pieces not to overlap.
Split, check the pieces are disjoint, add their chances, then rearrange.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the split of $\{X \le b\}$, and finish with the formula.

byKey.add: Adding chances needs disjoint pieces, so the disjoint line must come first.
byKey.solve: The formula is the end of the argument, not its start.

explain.text: $\{X \le b\}$ splits into two disjoint pieces at $a$, so their chances add. Rearranging gives $F(b) - F(a)$. The piece $a < X$ excludes $a$, which is why $F(4) - F(2)$ lost $Y = 2$.

screens.prose: A trading desk models its daily loss $L$ in £ thousands with the pmf below. Risk managers read losses from the CDF.

state.caption: A negative loss is a gain

screens.question: Fill in the CDF column, $F(\ell) = P(L \le \ell)$.

hints.text: Each $F$ is the one above it plus the new bar.
Start from $F(-2) = 0.30$ and add $p(0) = 0.25$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a running total of the $p$ column.

byKey.r6c2: The last value of a CDF is always 1.

explain.text: Each row adds one bar to the row above, so $F$ climbs 0.30, 0.55, 0.75, 0.90, 0.96, 0.99 and 1.00. It never falls, and it ends at 1. A loss of £2k or less has chance 0.90.

screens.prose: The desk's 95% value at risk (VaR) is the smallest loss level $x$ with $F(x) \ge 0.95$. On at least 95% of days the loss is at most this.
screens.question: What is the 95% VaR, in £ thousands?

hints.text: Go down the $F$ column. Where does it first reach 0.95?
Look at the rows for £2k and £5k.
$F(2) = 0.90$ is short of 0.95. $F(5) = 0.96$ reaches it, so the VaR is £5k.

feedback.correct: $F$ first reaches 0.95 at a loss of £5k.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first row whose $F$ is at least 0.95.

byKey.below: $F(2) = 0.90$, which is below 0.95. On 10% of days the loss exceeds £2k.
byKey.past: $F(5) = 0.96$ already reaches 0.95. You want the smallest such level.
byKey.worst: That is the worst loss in the model. VaR at 95% ignores the worst 5% of days.

explain.text: $F(2) = 0.90$ falls short and $F(5) = 0.96$ clears 0.95, so the 95% VaR is £5k. $L$ takes no value between 2 and 5, so $F$ jumps straight past 0.95. For a discrete loss the quantile sits on a jump.

ideas: The CDF $F(x) = P(X \le x)$ adds the pmf from the left, up to and including $x$.
For a discrete $X$ it is a staircase: flat between values, jumping by $p(x)$ at each value, rising from 0 to 1.
Chances come from differences: $P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)$ and $P(X > x) = 1 - F(x)$.

formula.name: Cumulative distribution function
formula.note: The closed dot sits on the upper step: at a value, $F$ already includes it.

summary.trap: $F(b) - F(a)$ leaves out $X = a$. For $P(2 \le Y \le 4)$, subtract $F(1)$, not $F(2)$.

quiz.question: Which list could be $F(1)$, $F(2)$, $F(3)$?

options.why: $F$ fell from 0.6 to 0.5. A CDF only adds chance as $x$ grows, so it never decreases.
$X$ is always at most 3, so $F(3)$ must be 1. Here 0.1 of the chance is missing.
That reads like a pmf, and it falls. A CDF climbs to 1.

feedback.correct: It never falls and it ends at 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A CDF never decreases and reaches 1 at the largest value.

explain.text: A CDF adds bars as $x$ moves right, so it never decreases. Past the largest value every bar is in, so it equals 1. Far to the left it is 0.

quiz.question: What is $P(X = 2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $P(X = 2)$ is the size of the jump at 2.

byKey.low: That is $F(1)$, the height before the jump.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the values of $X$ that are strictly below 2.

byKey.le: That is $F(2) = P(X \le 2)$. The strict sign leaves out $X = 2$ and its 0.5.

explain.text: For a discrete $X$, $P(X < 2)$ and $P(X \le 2)$ differ by $P(X = 2) = 0.5$. Only $X = 1$ is below 2, so the answer is $F(1) = 0.2$.

quiz.prose: The desk's daily loss $L$ in £ thousands has this pmf and CDF. Its loss limit is £2k.
quiz.question: What is the chance of a loss worse than the limit, $P(L > 2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take $F(2)$ away from 1.

byKey.height: That is $F(2)$, the chance of staying within the limit.
byKey.ge: That is $1 - F(1) = P(L \ge 2)$. A loss of exactly £2k is not worse than the limit.
byKey.past-five: That is $P(L > 5)$. Losses of £5k also break a £2k limit.
